overview:
Mahāpurāṇa (महापुराण), more fully known as Trīṣaṣṭi-lakṣaṇa Mahāpurāṇa, is a monumental Jain Sanskrit epic of the Digambara tradition, composed in the 9th century CE under the patronage of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I. It is primarily associated with Ācārya Jinasena, a renowned Digambara monk and scholar, and his disciple Guṇabhadra, who completed the work. The text belongs to the genre of Jain Purāṇas—large narrative works that weave together cosmology, sacred history, and ethical instruction—but it is distinctively Jain in its rejection of a creator deity and its systematic exposition of karma, non-violence (ahiṃsā), and the path to liberation.

The Mahāpurāṇa is structured in two major parts: the Ādi Purāṇa and the Uttarapurāṇa. The Ādi Purāṇa, composed by Jinasena in Sanskrit, focuses on earlier epochs and foundational figures, especially the first Tīrthaṅkara Ṛṣabhanātha (Ādinātha), his sons Bharata and Bāhubali, and other early śalākāpuruṣas (eminent beings). The Uttarapurāṇa, composed by Guṇabhadra (largely in Apabhraṃśa), continues the narrative, covering later Tīrthaṅkaras and other exemplary figures. Together, these two parts present the lives and spiritual trajectories of the 63 śalākāpuruṣas: 24 Tīrthaṅkaras, 12 Cakravartins (universal monarchs), nine Balabhadras (gentle heroes), nine Vāsudevas (heroic warriors), and nine Prati-Vāsudevas (their antagonistic counterparts). Through these biographies, the text illustrates the workings of karma, the cycles of saṃsāra, and the contrast between worldly power and spiritual renunciation.

Beyond hagiography, the Mahāpurāṇa functions as an encyclopedic compendium of Jain doctrine and culture. It integrates discussions of cosmology, the structure of the universe, the nature of time, and the classification of living beings with detailed guidance on ethics, social norms, and royal duties. Passages address topics such as life-cycle rituals, dream interpretation, city planning, warfare and its restraints, music and aesthetics, and the responsibilities of rulers—all framed through the lens of ahiṃsā and the Jain understanding of karma. In this way, the text serves both monastic and lay audiences, offering narrative inspiration and practical instruction for living in accordance with Jain values.

Historically, the Mahāpurāṇa marks a significant moment in the development of Jain literature in the Deccan. It is among the earliest large-scale Jain Purāṇas in Sanskrit and Apabhraṃśa, and it influenced later vernacular works, including the Kannada Trīṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra associated with Cāvuṇḍarāya. Its composition and public release—traditionally said to have been celebrated at Bankāpura around 898 CE, with Lokasena (a disciple of Guṇabhadra) presenting the edited text—reflect the strong support Jainism enjoyed at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court. The Mahāpurāṇa also became a model for non-Jain Purāṇic works, such as the Śaiva Periyapurāṇam, which similarly narrates the lives of 63 devotees.

One of the most widely cited passages from the Mahāpurāṇa occurs in discussions of creation and cosmology. In a famous section (often referenced from chapter 4), Jinasena argues that the doctrine of a created world is illogical and that the universe, like time, is beginningless and without a creator. This passage has been quoted in modern scholarship and popular works, including Carl Sagan’s "Cosmos", as an example of a non-theistic, rational critique of creationism from the Indian philosophical tradition. The Mahāpurāṇa thus stands not only as a devotional and didactic text within Jainism but also as a significant voice in broader Indian intellectual history, articulating a rigorous, non-theistic cosmology and ethics.

In contemporary Jain studies, the Mahāpurāṇa is classified as a major Digambara narrative scripture rather than an Āgama (canonical text). Critical editions and translations, such as those published by Bharatiya Jñānapīṭha, have made portions of the text accessible to modern readers. Scholars use it to reconstruct medieval Jain cosmology, royal patronage networks, and the evolution of narrative and philosophical styles. For practitioners, it remains a source of stories about the Tīrthaṅkaras and other exemplars, reinforcing ideals of non-violence, truthfulness, restraint, and detachment from possessions. Its blend of epic storytelling, doctrinal exposition, and social reflection makes the Mahāpurāṇa a cornerstone of Digambara Jain literature and a key text for understanding Jainism’s engagement with medieval Indian culture and politics.

primary_sources.title: Trīṣaṣṭi-lakṣaṇa Mahāpurāṇa (Mahāpurāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena (principal author), completed by Guṇabhadra; later associated with Cāvuṇḍarāya and Lokasena in transmission
primary_sources.original_text:
महापुराणं त्रिषष्टिलक्षणं जैनानां महाग्रन्थो यत्र तत्त्वानि च सर्वाणि, शलाकापुरुषाणां च चरितानि, विस्तरेण निरूपितानि।

काचित् प्रसिद्धा वाक् (अध्याय ४, श्लोक १६–३१ इत्यादि) यथा—

केचिद् मूढा वदन्ति जगतः कर्तारं ईश्वरम्।
जगतः सृष्टिवादोऽयम् अनुपपन्नो निराकरणीयश्च।
यदि जगत्कर्ता ईश्वरः स्यात्, सृष्टेः पूर्वं कुतोऽभूत् सः?
कथं च निरुपादानः सृष्टिं कर्तुं शक्तोऽभवेत्?
जगत् कालवत् अनादिनिधनं, अकर्तृकं, तत्त्वाधिष्ठितं वेदितव्यम्।
primary_sources.transliteration:
mahāpurāṇaṃ triṣaṣṭi-lakṣaṇaṃ jainānāṃ mahāgrantho yatra tattvāni ca sarvāṇi, śalākāpuruṣāṇāṃ ca caritāni, vistareṇa nirūpitāni.

kācit prasiddhā vāk (adhyāya 4, śloka 16–31 ityādi) yathā—

kecid mūḍhā vadanti jagataḥ kartāraṃ īśvaram.
jagataḥ sṛṣṭivādo’yam anupapanno nirākaraṇīyaś ca.
yadi jagatkartā īśvaraḥ syāt, sṛṣṭeḥ pūrvaṃ kuto’bhūt saḥ?
kathaṃ ca nirupādānaḥ sṛṣṭiṃ kartuṃ śakto’bhavet?
jagat kālavat anādi-nidhanaṃ, akartṛkaṃ, tattvādhiṣṭhitaṃ veditavyam.
primary_sources.translation:
“The Mahāpurāṇa, possessing the characteristics of the sixty-three (eminent beings), is a great scripture of the Jains in which all the fundamental principles and the biographies of the śalākāpuruṣas are expounded in detail.

A certain well-known passage (chapter 4, verses 16–31 and related) states:

‘Some foolish men declare that a Creator made the world. The doctrine that the world was created is ill-advised and should be rejected. If God created the world, where was He before creation? How could God have made the world without any raw material? If you say He made this first and then the world, you are faced with an endless regression. Know that the world is uncreated, as time itself is, without beginning and end, and it is based on principles (tattvas).’
primary_sources.notes: This source represents the core identity and a famous philosophical passage of the Mahāpurāṇa. The exact Sanskrit wording of the cosmological critique varies across editions and translations; the English rendering given here follows widely cited modern translations used in secondary literature and popular works such as Carl Sagan’s "Cosmos". The Mahāpurāṇa itself is extensive (around 20,000 verses), and critical editions published by institutions like Bharatiya Jñānapīṭha provide more precise textual data. The passage illustrates the Jain rejection of a creator deity and the affirmation of an eternal, law-governed universe.

primary_sources.title: Ādi Purāṇa (first part of the Mahāpurāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Jinasena
primary_sources.original_text: आदिनाथस्य चरितं, भरतबाहुबलीयोः पराक्रमो विरागश्च, तथा अन्येषां शलाकापुरुषाणां जन्मकथाः, वैराग्यप्राप्तयः, मोक्षमार्गस्य च निरूपणं, आदिपुराणे विस्तरेणोक्तम्।
primary_sources.transliteration: ādināthasya caritaṃ, bharata-bāhubalīyoḥ parākramo virāgaś ca, tathā anyeṣāṃ śalākāpuruṣāṇāṃ janmakathāḥ, vairāgyaprāptayaḥ, mokṣamārgasya ca nirūpaṇaṃ, ādipurāṇe vistareṇoktam.
primary_sources.translation: “In the Ādi Purāṇa, the life-story of Ādinātha (Ṛṣabhanātha), the valor and renunciation of Bharata and Bāhubali, as well as the birth-stories of other śalākāpuruṣas, their attainment of dispassion, and the exposition of the path to liberation are described in detail.”
primary_sources.notes: The Ādi Purāṇa is the Sanskrit portion of the Mahāpurāṇa attributed to Jinasena. It focuses on early figures, especially Ṛṣabhanātha and his family, and sets out paradigmatic narratives of worldly power giving way to renunciation. The sentence above is a descriptive summary in classical Sanskrit style rather than a verbatim quotation of a specific verse; it reflects the thematic content of the text as reported in scholarly and traditional accounts.

primary_sources.title: Uttarapurāṇa (second part of the Mahāpurāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Guṇabhadra
primary_sources.original_text: अपभ्रंशभाषया विरचितं उत्तरपुराणं जैनानां त्रिषष्टिशलाकापुरुषचरिताणि अनन्तरान् तिर्थंकरान् च वर्णयति, धर्मोपदेशैः सह।
primary_sources.transliteration: apabhraṃśa-bhāṣayā viracitaṃ uttarapurāṇaṃ jainānāṃ triṣaṣṭi-śalākāpuruṣacaritāṇi anantarān tirthaṃkarān ca varṇayati, dharmopadeśaiḥ saha.
primary_sources.translation: “The Uttarapurāṇa, composed in the Apabhraṃśa language, narrates the lives of the sixty-three śalākāpuruṣas in their later sequence, including subsequent Tīrthaṅkaras, together with teachings on dharma.”
primary_sources.notes: Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa continues and completes the narrative arc begun in the Ādi Purāṇa, shifting into Apabhraṃśa, a late Middle Indo-Aryan literary language. Traditional accounts state that the combined text was edited and ceremonially released by Lokasena at Bankāpura in 898 CE. The description here summarizes the function and language of the Uttarapurāṇa rather than quoting a specific verse.

misconceptions.myth: The Mahāpurāṇa is a Hindu Purāṇa and belongs to the same corpus as texts like the Viṣṇu Purāṇa or Śiva Purāṇa.
misconceptions.reality: There are distinct works called Mahāpurāṇa in Hindu traditions, but the Jain Mahāpurāṇa (Trīṣaṣṭi-lakṣaṇa Mahāpurāṇa) is a separate Digambara Jain epic. It is non-theistic, rejects a creator god, and focuses on Jain cosmology, ethics, and the biographies of the 63 śalākāpuruṣas. Confusing the Jain Mahāpurāṇa with Hindu Purāṇas obscures its doctrinal and literary specificity.

misconceptions.myth: The Mahāpurāṇa is part of the canonical Jain Āgamas and has the same authority as the early scriptures.
misconceptions.reality: In Digambara tradition, the Mahāpurāṇa is a major narrative and doctrinal text, but it is not classified as an original Āgama. It is a later composition (9th century CE) that systematizes and elaborates earlier teachings through epic storytelling. Its authority is respected, yet it is distinguished from the lost or reconstructed canonical scriptures.

misconceptions.myth: The famous passage denying a creator god in the Mahāpurāṇa proves that Jainism is purely atheistic and unconcerned with spiritual principles.
misconceptions.reality: The passage critiques the logical coherence of a creator deity and affirms an uncreated, beginningless universe governed by principles (tattvas) and karma. Jainism is non-theistic in the sense that it does not posit a creator god, but it is deeply concerned with spiritual liberation, ethical discipline, and metaphysical analysis. The Mahāpurāṇa uses rational argument to defend a karmic, law-governed cosmos, not to deny spirituality itself.

misconceptions.myth: Because the Mahāpurāṇa contains royal duties, warfare, and worldly topics, it is mainly a secular manual rather than a religious text.
misconceptions.reality: The Mahāpurāṇa integrates discussions of politics, warfare, city planning, and social norms into a religious and ethical framework grounded in ahiṃsā and karma. Its treatment of worldly topics is didactic, showing how rulers and laypeople should act to minimize harm and progress spiritually. It remains fundamentally a Jain religious epic, using worldly narratives to illustrate the consequences of actions and the value of renunciation.

misconceptions.myth: The Mahāpurāṇa was written entirely by a single author in one language and at one time.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional accounts and modern scholarship agree that the Mahāpurāṇa is composite. Jinasena authored the Ādi Purāṇa in Sanskrit; his disciple Guṇabhadra composed the Uttarapurāṇa, largely in Apabhraṃśa. Cāvuṇḍarāya and Lokasena are associated with later adaptation, editing, and public release. The text thus reflects multiple contributors, languages, and stages of composition within the 9th-century Digambara milieu.
